title: Arboles Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Arboles wells have a 140-foot median depth, 7 gpm median yield, and typical completed costs of $15,100-$26,000.
h1: What Arboles Wells Cost, Produce, and Require
intro_html:
Buying land around Arboles means buying into a mountain-bedrock water setting. Colorado DWR records within 5 miles show 506 permitted wells, with 357 recorded as constructed. Of those, 289 report a total depth, 56 report a pump yield, and 21 report a static water level.

The records point to generally moderate well depths and usable reported yields, but the local ground is fractured bedrock. That makes the neighboring well map useful for planning, not a guarantee for a particular lot. A driller still needs to evaluate access, geology, casing, grout, pump design, and the permit before giving a firm proposal.

sections.heading: Arboles well depths reflect fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Arboles is 140 feet, and the middle half runs from 100 to 200 feet. About 70% of the wells fall between 100 and 300 feet, while 25% are under 100 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 244 feet.

That range is a reasonable starting point for a drilling estimate, not a promise about a specific parcel. Fractured granite and gneiss can produce water through isolated fractures, so nearby wells may differ substantially. The deepest well on record is 2,950 feet, showing that exceptions exist. A contractor bidding your lot should review nearby completions, access, proposed casing and grout, and the well permit conditions before setting a final depth allowance.

sections.heading: Reported Arboles yields are usually workable, but not uniform
sections.html:
Among the 56 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 4.4 to 12.2 gallons per minute. The records show 52% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, 21% at 15 gallons per minute or more, and 27% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

No reported well in this data set is under 1 gallon per minute. That is encouraging for a buyer, but the yield sample is much smaller than the total permit record. Well yield is not the same as storage in the pressure tank or household use at one moment. Ask for the completion report and pump test, then match the system to the home, fixtures, irrigation plans, and any livestock use.

sections.heading: Arboles water levels show a shallow reported static range, not a trend
sections.html:
The 21 wells reporting static water level have a median depth to water of 42 feet, with the middle half from 21 to 62 feet. That can help a driller think about pump setting, trenching, and initial system design, but it does not establish the water level on an unbuilt lot.

The permit count rises from 2 in the 1950s to 142 in the 2010s, with 24 permits in the 2020s and the newest permit year recorded as 2025. Those figures describe permitting activity, not a falling or rising water table. Because fractured-bedrock wells may draw from separate water-bearing fractures, a nearby static reading should be treated as local evidence rather than a basin-wide forecast.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Arboles, and when permits were issued
sections.html:
Domestic and household wells make up 69% of the nearby permit records. Stock and irrigation wells each account for 3%, while monitoring wells account for 1%. The named aquifer is usually unnamed or fractured bedrock, covering 472 wells. Fruitland-Pictured Cliffs appears on 19 permits, alluvial aquifers on 4, and Denver Basin aquifers on 0.

The most active drillers in these records are Mortimer Water Well Drilling, also listed as Mortimer, Harry, with 53 wells; Beeman Bros Drilling Inc, also listed as Beeman, J. L., with 33; and Dak Drilling LLC, also listed as Rathjen, Doug, with 31. Records reach back to the 1950s and include a newest permit year of 2025. Verify current licensing, insurance, scope, and references before hiring.

sections.heading: What an Arboles well may cost to drill and finish
sections.html:
For fractured mountain bedrock such as granite and gneiss, the local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 140-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $9,100 to $14,000. That is only the hole and should not be mistaken for a ready-to-use water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $15,100 to $26,000 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing, longer trenching, or challenging electrical work can change the bid. Request a written allowance that separates drilling, casing and grout, development, pump equipment, storage, trenching, electrical, testing, and permit-related work.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Arboles
sections.html:
The primary water risk is variability. Although no reported well in this set is under 1 gallon per minute, only 56 wells report a pump yield, and fractured rock can produce a dry hole or a low-producing fracture on one parcel while a nearby well performs well. Review neighboring permits and completion reports before closing, and make the contract contingencies fit the actual water plan.

Environmental review also matters. There are 6 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles. There are 0 historic mine features and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the mapped data. Test existing water for common drinking-water concerns and any site-specific concern identified during due diligence. Confirm septic setbacks, drainfield space, driveway access, electrical routing, and building location before drilling or excavating.

sections.heading: A practical lot plan for Southern Ute and nearby Arboles areas
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit record for the parcel and nearby wells, especially completions showing depth, yield, static level, aquifer description, casing, and grout. Use the 100-to-200-foot middle depth range and 4.4-to-12.2-gpm middle yield range as planning context, then have a licensed driller inspect the site and access route.

Confirm the proposed domestic use, tank capacity, pump setting, septic layout, and electrical service before construction begins. An exempt household-use well can have specific legal limits; Colorado’s exempt-well pumping limit is 35 gallons per minute, and an augmentation plan may be required in an over-appropriated basin. Have the title, permit, water quality, and building plans reviewed together rather than treating the well as a separate item.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Arboles, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Arboles is 140 feet, with the middle half from 100 to 200 feet. About 70% are between 100 and 300 feet, but the deepest record is 2,950 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock makes the neighboring records useful for estimating, not guaranteeing, a depth on your lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Arboles?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite and gneiss. At the 140-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $9,100 to $14,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $15,100 to $26,000. Access, depth, casing, and site conditions can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water does an Arboles well produce?
faq.a: The 56 nearby wells reporting pump yield have a median of 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 4.4 to 12.2 gallons per minute. Reported yields range across the area: 27% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, 52% between 5 and 15, and 21% at 15 or more.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Arboles?
faq.a: The permit records do not prove that water is safe to drink. There are 6 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, so testing is important, especially near a site identified during due diligence. Test an existing or new well for routine drinking-water concerns and discuss any location-specific testing with a qualified professional.

faq.q: Are Arboles wells running out of water?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a declining water table. Reported static water levels have a 42-foot median, with the middle half from 21 to 62 feet, but only 21 wells report that measurement. Permit activity increased through the 2010s, yet permit counts are not water-level measurements. Review nearby static readings and pumping information for the specific property.
